## Context resolved (Step 0 pass)

The killer is IDENTIFIED from evidence already on the box — recorded here so the
planner inherits it rather than re-deriving it.

**Prime suspect confirmed: `earlyoom` under its blanket python `--prefer` bonus.**

1. VM timezone is `America/Los_Angeles` (PDT, UTC-7), so journal local times map
   directly onto the body's UTC incident stamps.
2. Window A — body reports `issue2221_build_mix.py` attempt 1 died rc=143 at
   16:24:40Z. The earlyoom unit journal has, at `Aug 13 09:24:40` PDT (= the same
   second): `mem avail: 12849 of 128804 MiB (9.98%)`, `low memory! at or below
   SIGTERM limits`, then `sending SIGTERM to process 1838073 uid 1001 "python3":
   badness 972, VmRSS 1054 MiB`. Same second, same signal, matching victim class.
3. Window B — body reports two `scripts/file_infra_task.py` kills at ~00:42-44Z on
   2026-08-14 (= 17:42-44 PDT on 08-13). The journal shows a sustained sweep across
   that window: `"python"` at badness 973 (VmRSS 1395 MiB), then `"python3"` at
   badness 966 (VmRSS 53 MiB), 966 (48 MiB), and a `chrome` at 800 — all SIGTERM,
   all inside 11 seconds, with MemAvailable oscillating at 9.47-10.00%.
4. Mechanism — live config `/etc/default/earlyoom`:
   `EARLYOOM_ARGS="-m 10 -s 10 -r 3600 --prefer (^|/)(pytest|python3?)$ --avoid (^|/)(sshd|systemd|dockerd|node|claude|happy)$|^[0-9]+[.][0-9]+[.][0-9]+$ -n"`.
   The `--prefer` +300 badness bonus applies to every process whose comm matches
   `pytest` / `python` / `python3`, which INVERTS size ordering: an observed 44 MiB
   python scores badness 966, beating a 3728 MiB java (686) and a 660 MiB Claude
   session (670). So under the 10%-MemAvailable floor every python on the box is a
   top-priority victim regardless of how small or short-lived it is.

**Why the body's own checks missed it (three traps to carry into the plan):**

- "No OOM (journalctl clean)" — the kernel OOM killer logs to dmesg with
  `oom_score`; earlyoom logs to its own unit journal with `badness`. A dmesg /
  kernel-log read structurally cannot see an earlyoom kill. (Already the documented
  protocol: `failure_patterns.md` § exit-137/143 step 3, `gotchas.md` line 61.)
- "53 GB free" is DISK; the binding quantity is MemAvailable, which was at 9.5-10.0%
  of 128 GB (~12.2-12.9 GB) in both windows.
- The `setsid`-survives / in-session-dies discriminator is almost certainly a
  CONFOUND, not a mechanism: earlyoom selects on badness and is session-agnostic —
  it never inspects session or process-group membership. earlyoom fires in bursts at
  the floor, so a rerun seconds-to-minutes later lands outside the sweep and
  survives. Any survive-vs-die A/B on this VM is uninterpretable unless both arms
  run inside one sweep window. This trap is what pointed the original triage at
  harness child-reaping / janitor pkill / systemd session cleanup.

**Prior-art / near-duplicate check (what is ALREADY covered — do not re-ship):**

- `.claude/rules/gotchas.md` line 60 already documents the 10%/5% floors, the
  `--prefer python3?` +300 bonus, the #811 collateral-kill variant, and the
  `choom -n -600` protection for sanctioned detached phases.
- `.claude/rules/gotchas.md` line 61 + `failure_patterns.md` § exit-137/143 already
  document the four-source kill-source checklist (kernel OOM / earlyoom /
  systemd-oomd cgroup / deliberate kill).
- The watcher already pre-attributes earlyoom kills as `kind=earlyoom-kill` rows in
  `.claude/cache/cpu-guard-events.jsonl` (#849).

Residual gap the task should close: (a) the badness INVERSION consequence is nowhere
stated — existing text says "+300 to every python" but never that size becomes nearly
irrelevant, which is exactly why a `--help` invocation dying "within seconds" read as

killed comm `python`); (c) the setsid-vs-in-session confound above.

**Scope constraint for the planner — the "stop it" half is USER-GATED.** The lever
that would actually stop these kills is a change to `/etc/default/earlyoom` (raise the
`-m`/`-s` floors, narrow or drop the blanket `--prefer` python bonus, add swap). That
is a sudo-level, fleet-wide, outside-the-worktree mutation on a shared VM
(halt-criterion #2, and CLAUDE.md's own rule that pods/system state are not

blast radius stated, parked for the user — never applied by this session. The
autonomously-shippable half is the in-repo workflow-surface fix (the three residual
facts above) plus any repro instrument.

MUST-FIX (accepted, claim INVERTED): plan v1 §2.6 asserted `choom -n -600` is VOID for
prefer-matched python, sourced from the man-page clause "for processes matched by --prefer,
negative oom_score_adj values are not taken into account". The critic read the installed
daemon's actual source and found the man page overstates. Independently re-verified by the
orchestrator before acceptance:
  - installed: earlyoom v1.6.2, Debian 1.6.2-1, plain upstream repack ("New upstream release",
    no patches per changelog.Debian.gz).
  - upstream v1.6.2 kill.c victim loop: `cur.badness = get_oom_score(cur.pid)` — the KERNEL
    oom_score, which DOES reflect a negative oom_score_adj — then `cur.badness += BADNESS_PREFER`
    (300) on a --prefer comm match, `+= BADNESS_AVOID` (-300) on --avoid. The only
    oom_score_adj handling is gated on `args->ignore_oom_score_adj` (the `-i` flag, NOT set in
    this VM's EARLYOOM_ARGS) and subtracts POSITIVE adj only. No code path discards a negative
    adj for prefer-matched processes.
  - measured on this box: choom -n -600 on a python3 moved kernel oom_score 666 -> 267.
  - therefore a choomed python scores 267 + 300 = 567, ~99 BELOW the flat ~666 baseline every
    unmatched process carries. choom -600 remains PROTECTIVE for python, attenuated by the +300
    — it moves a python from always-first-victim (966) to below the entire unmatched crowd.
  - corroboration: across all 650 logged victim kills (Aug 13-14) the badness distribution
    bottoms out at 669 — no victim was ever selected below the unmatched baseline. Weak-form
    (cannot distinguish "choomed procs were protected" from "no choomed proc was present"); the
    source read is the load-bearing evidence.
